message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) are both placental mammals, but they belong to different orders—Carnivora for lions and Perissodactyla for zebras.  
Their last common ancestor was a small, insectivorous mammal that lived roughly 60–70 million years ago during the Paleocene/Eocene transition. This ancestor belonged to the clade **Laurasiatheria**, which is part of the larger group of placental mammals (Eutheria). In other words, the common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, early Laurasiatherian mammal that eventually gave rise to the distinct lineages that became the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla.

Zebras are in order Perissodactyla, family Equidae. They diverged earlier. The common ancestor would be a mammal from the clade Laurasiatheria? Actually, lions and zebras are both mammals, but they belong to different orders: Carnivora and Perissodactyla. Their last common ancestor would be a mammal from the clade Laurasiatheria, perhaps a mammal from the clade that gave rise to the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That ancestor would be a mammal from the clade that includes the orders Carnivora, Perissodactyla, Artiodactyla, Chiroptera, Cetartiodactyla, etc. The last common ancestor of all these orders is a mammal from the clade Laurasiatheria, which is part of the clade Eutheria (placental mammals). So the common ancestor would be a placental mammal from the clade Laurasiatheria, likely a small, insectivorous mammal from the Paleocene or early Eocene. But the question might be simpler: The common ancestor of lions and zebras is a mammal from the clade that gave rise to the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. So we can answer: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, insectivorous mammal that lived around 60-70 million years ago, belonging to the clade Laurasiatheria. Or we can say: The common ancestor is a mammal from the clade that gave rise to the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is part of the clade Laurasiatheria. So we can answer accordingly.
